title: The Code Basis Is Four Answers Given in Order
summary: Before a building can be designed, four code questions must be answered in order: what is it used for, what is it built of, how tall and large may it be, and how do different uses inside it relate. Those answers, the code basis, decide structure, fire protection, cost and even what you can sell. Change one late and the others move with it.
body:
Every building code question you will face sits on four answers, given in order: the occupancy, the construction type, the allowable height and area, and how mixed uses are handled. Write those four answers down before design starts, because changing any one of them later redesigns the building.

Recall

Q. In a flood zone, what is a breakaway wall?

A. A wall below the elevated floor designed to collapse under flood forces without damaging the structure, so waves pass beneath the building.

Q. In design management, what is a design brief?

A. The owner's written statement of what the building must achieve: uses, areas, quality, budget, programme and performance targets, against which every design stage is checked.

Q. Why might someone hold assets in two countries under two wills, in concept?

A. So that each will can be probated locally under the law where the assets sit, which can be faster and simpler. The wills must be drafted together so one does not revoke the other; verify that against the primary source and a qualified lawyer in each place.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the building code is the single document that most constrains what you can build, and it is organised around these four answers. Owners who treat the code as the architect's problem discover, at permit, that the building they priced is not the building the code allows. Owners who understand the four answers can test a concept in an hour and know what to ask their architect and code consultant. This week Ivo teaches the code basis using the International Building Code (IBC), the model code adopted across most of the United States.

Answer one: what is the building used for

In plain English: the code sorts buildings by how people use them, because a sleeping person, a shopper and a factory worker face fire differently.

The professional framing is the occupancy classification: the use group the code assigns to a building or part of one. Residential groups are the ones you will meet most. In the IBC, group R-1 covers transient residential uses such as hotels and motels, where occupants stay a short time and do not know the building; group R-2 covers apartments and condominiums with more than two dwelling units, where occupants are primarily permanent. The code defines transient by length of stay, commonly 30 days or less [unverified — confirm independently]. Other groups matter in a mixed building: assembly for restaurants and event spaces, business for offices, mercantile for shops, storage for parking garages.

Worked example 1, hypothetical. You plan furnished units let by the month. If guests typically stay under the transient threshold, the building official may class it R-1 rather than R-2. That can change the number of accessible guest rooms, the fire alarm features in each unit, and whether federal accessibility rules for places of lodging apply, as well as your zoning, insurance and lending. The same floor plan, two different buildings in law. Decide the real business model first, then classify honestly.

Answer two: what is it built of

In plain English: the code sorts buildings by how much their structure resists fire and whether it burns.

The IBC has five construction types. Types I and II use noncombustible materials such as concrete and protected steel. Type III has noncombustible exterior walls with interior structure that may be combustible. Type IV covers heavy timber and, in recent editions, mass timber. Type V allows any permitted material, typically light wood framing. Most types are subdivided into A, protected with fire-resistance-rated elements, and B, unprotected. The higher the type, the more the building may be allowed in height and area, and the more it costs to build [unverified — confirm independently].

Say that out loud now.

Occupancy, construction type, height and area, mixed use: four answers, in that order.

Answer three: how tall and how big

The IBC tables allowable height in feet, number of stories and area per story by occupancy and construction type, with increases for automatic sprinklers and for open frontage around the building [unverified — confirm independently]. A fire wall built to code can divide one structure into separate buildings for this purpose. These limits are why a concept that works in concrete may not work in wood, and why the same site can carry more floor area in one construction type than another.

Answer four: how the uses fit together

A building with shops below and homes above is a mixed occupancy. The IBC offers three main approaches [unverified — confirm independently]. Accessory occupancies, small areas subordinate to the main use, may be treated as part of it. Nonseparated occupancies apply the most restrictive requirements of all the uses throughout the building. Separated occupancies divide the uses with rated fire barriers or horizontal assemblies, and each part follows its own rules. Many podium buildings use a related provision that lets a lower level of noncombustible construction be treated as a separate building from the residential floors above [unverified — confirm independently].

Worked example 2, hypothetical. A building has a ground-floor restaurant and offices, with residential floors above. Treating it as nonseparated means the residential floors carry restaurant-level requirements everywhere that is stricter. Separating the restaurant with a rated fire barrier costs a few hundred thousand dollars in construction, and it may let the rest of the building use a cheaper construction type. That trade is an owner decision, priced on Day 3.

How the best do it

Disciplined owners hire a code consultant, or have their architect prepare a code analysis, at concept stage, and they put it on the cover sheet of every drawing issue: occupancy, construction type, allowable and actual height and area, sprinkler system, separations and the adopted code edition. Any change to those lines needs the owner's sign-off. A small developer can copy that discipline with a one-page code basis attached to the design brief.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: occupancy can affect how a property is classified for property tax and transaction taxes; verify that against the primary source. Liability: a building used outside its code classification exposes the owner if anyone is hurt. Banking: lenders lend on a permitted use, and a mismatch can be a loan default. Governance: only the owner approves a change to the code basis. Estate: an heir inherits the building's permitted use, not the use someone hoped for. Exit: a buyer's diligence checks that the certificate of occupancy matches the actual use.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is choosing the occupancy that makes the permit easiest rather than the one that matches how the building will be used and sold. The control is a written code basis that states the business model behind the occupancy choice, confirmed with the building official. Professional sign-off required: a registered architect and, on complex buildings, a licensed code consultant or fire protection engineer.

The beginner's mistake

Starting with height and area. Height and area depend on occupancy and construction type, so starting there gives a number with nothing under it.

Callback

In Week 29, Remi taught asset types and hotel metrics: average daily rate, occupancy, revenue per available room. Those revenue choices are also code choices. A building run as a hotel is a transient occupancy, and the code follows the business model whether you planned for it or not.

Recap

The code basis is four answers in order: occupancy, construction type, height and area, mixed use. Classify on the real business model, write the basis on one page, and own every change to it.

Next: Ford on Failure Forensics: a composite case of apartments that became a hotel without anyone telling the building code.
checklist: State the real business model, including typical length of stay, before choosing an occupancy.
Classify every part of the building by occupancy group.
Choose a construction type and record why.
Check allowable height, stories and area with the sprinkler and frontage increases.
Choose accessory, nonseparated or separated treatment for mixed uses and price the separations.
Name the adopted code edition and local amendments.
Put the code basis on the cover sheet of every drawing issue.
Get professional sign-off from a registered architect or code consultant.
head: Field checklist
speak: The code basis is four answers given in order. First, occupancy: what the building is used for. Hotels and other short stays are transient, group R-1; apartments and condominiums are group R-2, and the line is usually length of stay. Second, construction type: Types I and II noncombustible, Type III with noncombustible exterior walls, Type IV heavy or mass timber, Type V any permitted material, each split into protected and unprotected. Third, height and area: the code tables them by occupancy and type, with increases for sprinklers and open frontage, and fire walls can divide a structure. Fourth, mixed use: accessory, nonseparated, where the strictest rule applies everywhere, or separated by rated barriers. I classify on the real business model, write the four answers on one page, confirm them with the building official, and nobody changes them without my signature.
terms: Occupancy classification — the code's use group for a building or part of one, which drives most other requirements.
Construction type — the code's classification of a building by the fire resistance and combustibility of its structure.
Separated occupancies — a mixed-use approach in which uses are divided by rated fire barriers so each follows its own rules.

hostile.q: Your drawings classify the building as apartments, but your pro forma shows nightly rates. Which is it?
hostile.a: That mismatch is exactly what the code basis is meant to catch, so I will resolve it before the permit. If we intend short stays, the building is transient and the design changes: accessible guest rooms, alarm features and possibly the zoning and insurance. If we intend apartments, the pro forma must show monthly rents. I will not permit one use and operate another.

title: The Apartments That Became a Hotel
summary: This is a composite example. A building permitted as apartments was run as short-stay rentals, which the code treats as a different occupancy. When the building official noticed, the owner faced a change of occupancy, retrofit costs, a loan problem and an insurance gap. Seven steps show how a marketing decision became a code event.
body:
This is a composite example, drawn from a pattern rather than one real building. An owner changed how a building was used without telling the code, and discovered that the building he owned was not the building he had permission to run.

Recall

Q. What is the first of the four code-basis answers?

A. Occupancy: what the building is used for, which drives most other code requirements.

Q. What does an elevation certificate record?

A. A building's floor and equipment heights relative to the flood elevation, prepared by a licensed surveyor or engineer and used by insurers and the building official.

Q. What is a consultant scope gap?

A. A task that falls between consultants' written scopes so that no one is contracted to do it.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, short-stay rental income can be higher than long-term rent, and the temptation to switch is strong when a market softens or a platform makes it easy. The code, the zoning, the lender and the insurer all care about that switch. This case shows what happens when only the marketing team knows about it.

Step 1: The timeline

A developer built a mid-sized apartment building in a city centre, permitted as group R-2, residential non-transient. Lease-up was slow. In year two, the asset manager began letting furnished units by the night through online platforms, starting with ten units and growing to most of the building. Revenue rose. In year three, a fire in one unit, caused by a guest's cooking, was contained by the sprinklers but triggered a fire department report, which noted a reception desk, luggage storage and guests who did not know the exits. The building official opened a file. The owner received a notice that the building's use had changed to transient lodging without a permit.

Step 2: Key decisions

The key decision was made in a revenue meeting, not a design meeting: convert units to short stays to fill vacancy. No one asked the architect, the code consultant, the lender or the insurer. A second decision, to expand from ten units to most of the building, was made on revenue results alone.

Step 3: Assumptions

The asset manager assumed that a dwelling unit is a dwelling unit, whoever sleeps in it. The code does not agree. It classifies by how occupants use the building, and short stays make it transient, because guests are unfamiliar with the building and its exits.

Say that out loud now.

The code follows the business model, not the floor plan.

Step 4: Incentives

The asset manager was paid on revenue. The platform made conversion frictionless. No one was paid to check compliance, and the person who would have objected, the code consultant, was no longer on the team after completion.

Step 5: Warning signs ignored

The loan agreement's permitted-use clause. The insurance policy's description of the risk. A local short-term rental ordinance requiring registration. Neighbour complaints about luggage in corridors. A reception desk that turned a lobby into a hotel front office. Each was visible to someone, and no one put them together.

Step 6: Point of no return

The point of no return came when most of the building had converted and the revenue model depended on it. At ten units, the owner could have stopped quietly. At most of the building, stopping meant losing the income that now serviced the debt.

Step 7: Root cause

The root cause was that a use change was treated as an operating decision rather than a code, zoning, lending and insurance event. No one owned the question "is this still the building we have permission to run?"

The cost

Worked example 1, hypothetical round numbers. The building official required a change-of-occupancy permit under the existing building code adopted locally. The design review found the building needed more accessible guest rooms with specific features, changes to the fire alarm to suit transient sleeping rooms, and other upgrades. The retrofit cost 1,800,000 dollars, and units were off-line during the work. At 20 units off-line for 6 months at 3,000 dollars a month of net income each, that is another 360,000 dollars.

Worked example 2, hypothetical. The lender's loan agreement allowed residential leasing only. Short-stay operation without consent was an event of default. The lender did not foreclose, but it charged a consent fee of 0.5 percent on a 30,000,000-dollar loan, 150,000 dollars, increased the interest rate and required a hotel-operator agreement. Meanwhile the insurer reviewed the fire claim against a policy that described the risk as apartments; the claim was paid only after argument, and the renewal premium rose. The extra revenue from short stays, perhaps 600,000 dollars a year more than leasing, took years to recover these costs.

What should have happened

Before the first unit converted, the owner should have asked four people one question each. The code consultant: does this change our occupancy? The zoning lawyer: is short-stay use permitted here and does it need registration? The lender: does the loan allow it? The broker: does the policy cover it? With four answers in writing, the owner could have priced the conversion honestly, or decided against it.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is that a revenue decision quietly changes the building's legal identity. The control is a rule that any change in how a building is used, rented or marketed goes through a written code, zoning, loan and insurance check before it starts. Professional sign-off required: a registered architect or code consultant for the code, and a licensed lawyer for zoning and the loan.

The beginner's mistake

Assuming that a building, once permitted, can be used any way that fits inside it. A certificate of occupancy states a use, and the use is part of the permission.

Callback

In Week 39, Priya taught covenants and events of default in a construction loan. Permanent loans carry them too, and permitted-use clauses are among the easiest to break by accident. Read them before you change how a building earns its money.

Recap

A composite owner turned apartments into short stays, the code treated it as a change to transient occupancy, and the retrofit, the loan consent and the insurance gap cost more than the extra revenue for years. Treat use changes as code events first.

Rule 100: Classify the building on how it will actually be used, rented and sold, and treat any change of use as a code, zoning, loan and insurance event before it becomes a marketing decision.

Next: Priya on The Money: how construction type, height and area, and separations move cost, area and value.
checklist: Write down how each part of the building will be rented, including length of stay.
Check that the occupancy on the permit matches that business model.
Read the loan agreement's permitted-use clause before any change in operation.
Confirm the insurance policy describes the actual use.
Check local short-term rental and zoning rules before letting by the night.
Require a written code, zoning, loan and insurance check before any use change starts.
Keep a code consultant available after completion for use questions.
head: Field checklist
rule: Rule 100: Classify the building on how it will actually be used, rented and sold, and treat any change of use as a code, zoning, loan and insurance event before it becomes a marketing decision.
speak: This is a composite example. A building permitted as apartments, group R-2, was slowly converted to nightly rentals because lease-up was slow and revenue was better. Nobody asked the code consultant, the lender or the insurer. After a small fire, the building official found reception desks, luggage storage and guests unfamiliar with the exits, and treated it as an unpermitted change to transient occupancy. The owner faced a change-of-occupancy permit with accessibility and alarm retrofits, units off-line, a loan consent fee and a higher rate because the loan allowed residential leasing only, and an insurance argument because the policy described apartments. The root cause was treating a use change as an operating decision. Rule 100: classify the building on how it will actually be used, and treat any change of use as a code, zoning, loan and insurance event before it becomes a marketing decision.
terms: Change of occupancy — a change in how a building or space is used that moves it to a different code classification, usually requiring a permit.
Certificate of occupancy — the official document stating that a building may be occupied for a stated use.
Permitted-use clause — a loan or lease term limiting how the property may be used.

hostile.q: Your rent roll shows units let by the night. Has your building's occupancy been reviewed, and does your loan allow it?
hostile.a: Not yet, and I have stopped any further conversions until it is. I have asked our code consultant whether this is a transient occupancy, our lawyer to check zoning and the loan's permitted-use clause, and our broker to confirm cover. If the answers require a change-of-occupancy permit or a loan consent, I will bring you the cost and the plan before we continue.

title: How the Code Basis Moves Cost, Area and Value
summary: Construction type sets cost per square foot, height and area limits set how much you can build, and occupancy separations add cost or save it. Together they decide whether a concept is financeable. Price the code basis the way a lender does: cost per saleable square foot and value per dollar of equity.
body:
The code basis is a financial document in disguise. Construction type sets the cost of every square foot, height and area limits set how many square feet you may build, and the mixed-use approach adds or saves cost at every floor where uses meet.

Recall

Q. What is a change of occupancy?

A. A change in how a building or space is used that moves it to a different code classification, usually requiring a permit.

Q. What three things does resilience spending buy?

A. Expected loss avoided, downtime avoided, and cheaper insurance that improves debt service coverage and loan proceeds.

Q. What does BIM clash detection save money on?

A. Rework on site: it finds physical conflicts between systems in the model before they are built.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a lender sizes your loan on cost and value, and both move with the code basis. Two concepts for the same site can differ by millions in cost and in buildable area purely because of construction type and separations. If you can price those choices yourself, you can test a concept before paying for full design.

Construction type is a cost curve

In plain English: noncombustible construction lets you build bigger and taller, and costs more per square foot.

Light wood framing, Type V, is generally the cheapest structure per square foot and the most limited in height and area. Concrete or protected steel, Types I and II, is generally more expensive and less limited. Many mid-rise residential buildings combine them: a concrete podium for parking and retail, with wood framing above, so that each part uses the cheapest type the code allows for it [unverified — confirm independently]. These cost relationships are commercial observations that vary by market; your cost consultant supplies the numbers.

Worked example 1, hypothetical round numbers. A concept of 100,000 gross square feet. Option A, all concrete, at 320 dollars per square foot of structure and envelope: 32,000,000 dollars. Option B, a concrete podium of 30,000 square feet at 320 dollars and 70,000 square feet of wood framing above at 240 dollars: 9,600,000 plus 16,800,000, which is 26,400,000 dollars. Option B saves 5,600,000 dollars, if the code allows the wood-framed portion at the height and area you need. That "if" is the whole of Day 5.

Area you are allowed to build is revenue

In plain English: if the code caps a floor's area, every square foot above the cap is either lost or bought with a more expensive structure.

Worked example 2, hypothetical. A wood-framed scheme is capped at 24,000 square feet per floor; the site could hold 30,000. The 6,000 square feet lost per floor, at 80 percent efficiency, is 4,800 saleable square feet. At a hypothetical sale value of 500 dollars per square foot, that is 2,400,000 dollars of revenue per floor. Options: add a fire wall to create two buildings, each within its own cap; increase open frontage to raise the allowable area; or move up a construction type. If a fire wall costs 400,000 dollars and recovers the full area, it is the cheapest of the three by a wide margin.

Say that out loud now.

A code limit on area is a limit on revenue, so I price every way around it.

Separations cost money, and sometimes save more

Separated occupancies need rated fire barriers and protected openings between uses. That costs money at every interface. But separation can let each part of the building follow its own, often cheaper, rules. A restaurant left nonseparated may push restaurant-level requirements across the whole building. Price both ways before you choose. Professional sign-off required: a registered architect or code consultant on the code, and your cost consultant on the numbers.

How the lender sees it

A lender reads the code basis as risk. A scheme that depends on a variance, an alternative method approval or an untested interpretation is a scheme that may not be permitted as drawn, so the lender may hold back funding until the permit issues or ask for a larger contingency. Construction type also moves the insurance cost during construction: builder's risk premiums for wood framing are often materially higher than for concrete because of the fire risk before the building is finished. These are market practices, not standards, and they change with the insurance cycle. Ask your broker early.

Put the lender's numbers on the code choices. In worked example 1, Option B saves 5,600,000 dollars of cost. If builder's risk for Option B costs 300,000 dollars more and fire watch during framing costs another 100,000 dollars, the net saving is 5,200,000 dollars. If the lender lends 65 percent of cost, Option B also reduces the equity you must put in by 35 percent of 5,200,000 dollars, about 1,820,000 dollars. On the same land, the same revenue and less equity, the return on equity rises sharply. That is why the code basis belongs in the first conversation with the lender, not the last.

Wealth Ledger

Warrick's note for your personal balance sheet: equity you do not have to put into one building is equity available for the next one, or for the liquidity floor that protects you in a bad year. A code basis that saves cost without adding risk is one of the few ways to raise returns without raising leverage.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is pricing a concept on a construction type the code will not allow at that height and area. The control is a code analysis before the first cost estimate, signed off by the architect or code consultant, with the allowable height and area shown beside the actual.

The beginner's mistake

Comparing construction types on cost per square foot alone, without counting the area each type allows and the insurance and fire-watch costs during construction.

Callback

In Week 13, Sage taught sources and uses and the estimate classes. A code basis fixed at concept stage is what lets an early estimate stop moving: until the construction type is settled, the hard cost line is a guess.

Recap

Construction type sets cost per square foot, height and area limits set revenue, and separations trade cost for flexibility. Price each choice in cost, area, insurance and equity, and fix the code basis before the estimate.

Next: REGA on The Rules: how a model code becomes law, which edition applies, and who can approve a departure.
checklist: Get a code analysis before the first cost estimate.
Compare construction types on cost, allowable area, insurance and fire watch together.
Translate any area cap into lost saleable area and revenue.
Price every route around an area cap: fire wall, frontage, higher type.
Price separated and nonseparated treatment of mixed uses both ways.
Ask the broker for builder's risk premiums by construction type early.
Show the lender the code basis in the first meeting.
head: Field checklist
speak: The code basis is a financial document. Construction type sets cost per square foot: wood framing is cheaper and more limited, concrete costs more and allows more, and many buildings combine a concrete podium with wood above. On a hypothetical 100,000 square feet, that mix might save 5.6 million dollars against all concrete, if the code allows the wood at that height and area. Area limits are revenue limits: 6,000 square feet lost per floor can be millions of dollars of sales, so I price every way around the cap, a fire wall, more frontage, or a higher type. Separations cost money at each interface but can let each use follow cheaper rules. Lenders read code risk, and builder's risk insurance is often higher for wood. A cheaper code basis also cuts the equity I must put in, which raises return without raising leverage.
terms: Podium construction — a building with lower floors of noncombustible construction supporting a lighter structural type above.
Fire wall — a fire-resistance-rated wall that divides a structure into separate buildings for code purposes.
Builder's risk insurance — insurance covering a building under construction against physical loss such as fire.

hostile.q: Your cost plan assumes wood framing at a floor area I am told the code does not allow. Why should I lend on it?
hostile.a: You are right to ask, and I will not ask you to. Our code consultant's analysis shows the allowable area with sprinklers and frontage, and where the plan exceeds it, a rated fire wall divides the structure into two buildings within the limits. The fire wall is in the estimate, the builder's risk premium for wood is from the broker, and the analysis will be confirmed with the building official before we ask for the commitment.

title: Which Code, Which Edition, and Who Decides
summary: A model code has no force until a government adopts it, usually with amendments. The edition that governs your building is generally fixed by when you apply, and the building official interprets it. Learn the adoption chain, the role of the official, alternative methods and appeals, and the separate code for existing buildings.
body:
The International Building Code is not law until a state or city adopts it. What governs your building is a specific adopted edition with local amendments, read by a building official who has the authority to interpret it and to approve alternatives, subject to appeal.

Recall

Q. What is Rule 100?

A. Classify the building on how it will actually be used, rented and sold, and treat any change of use as a code, zoning, loan and insurance event before it becomes a marketing decision.

Q. What is a fire wall?

A. A fire-resistance-rated wall that divides a structure into separate buildings for code purposes.

Q. What does a commissioning intent document set out at design stage?

A. The owner's expectations for how building systems must perform and be tested, so that design and later commissioning share one target.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, two consultants can both say "the code requires" and mean different documents. One reads the newest model edition; the other reads the edition your city adopted years ago with local amendments. The difference can change construction type limits, sprinkler requirements or energy rules. You need to know which document governs and who has the last word.

From model code to law

In plain English: a private body writes the code, and governments make it law by adopting it.

The International Code Council publishes model codes on a regular cycle, including the building code, the fire code, the residential code, the existing building code and the energy conservation code. A state or local government adopts a chosen edition by statute or ordinance, often with amendments that add, delete or change provisions. The adopted text, not the model text, is the law. Many referenced standards, such as NFPA 13 for sprinklers or ASCE 7 for loads, become enforceable because the adopted code names a specific edition of them [unverified — confirm independently].

Worked example 1, hypothetical. Your architect designs to the newest model edition, which allows a mass-timber type at a greater height. Your city still enforces an older edition that does not. The design must be revised, or approved as an alternative, before permit. A month of redesign is cheap compared with a refused permit after full construction drawings.

Say that out loud now.

The adopted edition with local amendments governs, not the newest book on the shelf.

Which edition applies to you

Generally, a project is reviewed under the code in force when a complete permit application is submitted, though local rules on what counts as complete, how long an application stays valid, and how phased permits are handled vary [unverified — confirm independently]. When a new edition is about to be adopted, the date you file can decide your code basis. Ask the building department for its transition rules in writing.

The building official's authority

The code gives the building official, sometimes called the code official, authority to enforce it, to render interpretations, and to approve alternative materials, designs and methods of construction that are not specifically prescribed, provided the alternative is shown to be at least equivalent in quality, strength, effectiveness, fire resistance, durability and safety [unverified — confirm independently]. That equivalence is usually demonstrated by an engineer's analysis, test reports or evaluation reports. The official may approve, refuse or ask for more. This is where performance-based approaches enter, and Magnus returns to them in Week 102.

Worked example 2, hypothetical. Your design exceeds an allowable area by 5 percent. Instead of adding a fire wall at 400,000 dollars, your fire protection engineer proposes an alternative: enhanced sprinkler coverage and additional fire separations, supported by a written analysis. The official may accept it, refuse it, or accept it with conditions. If refused, you still need the fire wall, and you have lost the weeks spent on the proposal. Price an alternative as an option with a probability, never as a certainty.

Appeals

Most adopted codes provide a board of appeals to hear challenges to the official's decisions on interpretation or alternatives. An appeal is a formal proceeding on the merits of the code question, not a negotiation over cost, and the board generally cannot waive code requirements. Verify the procedure and timing locally. An appeal should be a last resort after a technical conversation has failed.

Existing buildings have their own code

Work on an existing building, including a change of occupancy, is often governed by the existing building code adopted locally rather than the new-construction code. It offers methods scaled to the scope of work, from repairs through alterations to change of occupancy, with requirements rising as the risk of the new use rises [unverified — confirm independently]. Day 2's composite case is a change of occupancy under that code. If you buy an older building to reposition, the existing building code is your first reading, not your last.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is designing to the wrong edition or assuming an alternative will be approved. The control is a written code basis naming the adopted editions and amendments, the filing date that fixes them, and every alternative proposed, each with a fallback design and its cost. Professional sign-off required: a registered architect and, for alternatives, a licensed fire protection or structural engineer.

The beginner's mistake

Treating the building official as an opponent. The official is the person who must sign your certificate of occupancy. A respectful, early, technical relationship is worth more than any argument at the counter.

Callback

In Week 25, LEX and Vera taught how to instruct professionals and challenge their advice. When two consultants disagree on what the code requires, the first question is which adopted edition each one read. That question settles more code disputes than any argument about interpretation.

Recap

Model codes become law by adoption with amendments. The edition in force at a complete application usually governs. The building official interprets and approves alternatives on demonstrated equivalence, subject to appeal. Existing buildings follow the existing building code. Write it all on one page with a fallback for every alternative.

Next: Ivo on The Numbers: reverse engineering a floor plate from the area the code allows.
checklist: Name the adopted building, fire and existing building code editions and local amendments.
Ask the building department for its edition transition rules in writing.
Confirm what counts as a complete permit application and when it vests.
List every proposed alternative method with its supporting analysis.
Price a fallback design for every alternative.
Use the existing building code first when repositioning an older building.
Treat an appeal as a last resort after a technical meeting.
Get sign-off from a registered architect and the relevant licensed engineer.
head: Field checklist
speak: A model code is not law until a government adopts it, usually with amendments, and the adopted text governs. Referenced standards like NFPA 13 and ASCE 7 become enforceable because the adopted code names their editions. The edition that applies is generally the one in force when a complete permit application is filed, so filing dates matter when a new edition is coming. The building official enforces the code, interprets it and may approve alternative materials and methods shown to be equivalent, usually with an engineer's analysis. I price every alternative as an option with a fallback design, never as a certainty. Appeals go to a board and are a last resort. Existing buildings and changes of occupancy are often governed by the existing building code. I keep one page naming the editions, amendments, filing date and every alternative.
terms: Adopted edition — the specific edition of a model code that a government has made law, with its local amendments.
Alternative materials and methods — a design not specifically prescribed by the code that the official may approve on demonstrated equivalence.
Existing building code — the code that governs repairs, alterations, additions and changes of occupancy in existing buildings, where adopted.

hostile.q: Your design relies on an alternative method the building official has not yet approved. What happens to my schedule if it is refused?
hostile.a: We carry a fallback design: the rated fire wall, already drawn and priced at about 400,000 dollars. The alternative saves that cost if approved, and our engineer's analysis goes to the official next week. If it is refused, we switch to the fallback within two weeks of the decision, and that time is already in the schedule contingency. Nothing in the critical path depends on approval.

title: Reverse Engineering a Floor Plate from the Area the Code Allows
summary: Start from the floor area you want and work backward to what the code would need: sprinklers, open frontage, construction type or a fire wall. Every table value here is invented for the exercise and labelled so, because the real values come from your adopted code.
body:
Instead of asking what the code allows on your site, start from the floor plate you want and work backward to what it would take: the frontage, the construction type, or the fire wall. Every table value below is invented for this exercise and is not the code's; the method is the lesson.

Recall

Q. Which edition of the building code generally applies to a project?

A. The adopted edition, with local amendments, in force when a complete permit application is filed, subject to local transition rules.

Q. What is the third of the four code-basis answers?

A. Height and area: how tall and how large the building may be for its occupancy and construction type.

Q. Why does a design flood elevation start with a datum?

A. Because every elevation must be measured from one stated reference, or consultants will build to different heights.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, you will often know the answer you want before you know the code: the site, the rents and the land price tell you how many square feet each floor must hold to make the deal work. Reverse engineering lets you see, before design, what the code would demand to give you that floor plate, and whether it is affordable.

The method in plain English

The IBC sets a tabular allowable area per story for each occupancy and construction type, with a higher value where the building is sprinklered. It then allows an increase where enough of the building's perimeter faces open space, such as a street or open yard of sufficient width. In concept, the allowable area per story is the tabular value plus an increase that grows with the open frontage [unverified — confirm independently]. One published form of that relationship, which your code consultant must confirm against your adopted edition, is:

Allowable area per story equals tabular area plus the nonsprinklered tabular area times the frontage increase factor, and the frontage increase factor equals the open frontage divided by the perimeter, minus 0.25, times the open width divided by 30 [unverified — confirm independently].

Say that out loud now.

Start from the floor plate I need, then solve for the frontage, the type or the fire wall that would allow it.

Worked example 1: solving for frontage

This is a hypothetical building, not your project. The target floor plate is 30,000 square feet, a rectangle 150 feet by 200 feet, so the perimeter is 2 times 150 plus 2 times 200, which is 700 feet. Suppose, for this exercise only, that the chosen occupancy and construction type give a sprinklered tabular area of 24,000 square feet and a nonsprinklered tabular area of 12,000 square feet. These are invented numbers.

Step 1: the shortfall. 30,000 minus 24,000 is 6,000 square feet that must come from the frontage increase.

Step 2: the factor needed. 6,000 divided by the nonsprinklered value of 12,000 gives a required frontage increase factor of 0.5.

Step 3: solve for frontage. Assume the open spaces are 30 feet wide, so the width term is 30 divided by 30, which is 1. Then 0.5 equals frontage over perimeter minus 0.25, so frontage over perimeter must be 0.75.

Step 4: convert to feet. 0.75 times 700 is 525 feet. At least 525 of the 700 feet of perimeter must face qualifying open space at least 30 feet wide.

Step 5: check the site. Suppose the site has a street on one long side and one short side, 200 plus 150, which is 350 feet. Frontage over perimeter is 0.5, so the factor is 0.5 minus 0.25, which is 0.25, and the increase is 12,000 times 0.25, which is 3,000 square feet. Allowable area per story is 27,000 square feet, 3,000 short of the target.

Worked example 2: pricing the routes to the last 3,000 square feet

Route A: create more open frontage by leaving a 30-foot open yard along a third side, 200 feet long. Frontage becomes 550 feet; 550 over 700 is about 0.79, the factor is about 0.54 and the increase is about 6,480 square feet. Allowable area is about 30,480 square feet, enough. But the yard consumes 30 times 200, or 6,000 square feet of site, which may cost more in lost land use than it gains.

Route B: a fire wall that divides the floor plate into two buildings of 15,000 square feet each, each well inside its own allowable area. Suppose it costs 400,000 dollars across the floors, plus some lost flexibility in layout.

Route C: move to a higher construction type with a larger tabular area. Suppose, again invented, that it gives a sprinklered tabular value of 36,000 square feet, but costs 40 dollars more per square foot on 100,000 gross square feet, which is 4,000,000 dollars.

Route D: shrink the floor plate to 27,000 square feet and accept 3,000 fewer square feet per floor.

Compare them in money. On Day 3's hypothetical value of 500 dollars per saleable square foot at 80 percent efficiency, the 3,000 square feet are worth 1,200,000 dollars per floor. Route B at 400,000 dollars recovers it for the whole building; Route C costs ten times as much; Route D loses the revenue; Route A depends on what the land is worth. On these numbers, the fire wall wins, subject to layout and to confirmation of every value against the adopted code.

Check height as well

Area is only half of the third answer. The code also limits height in feet and number of stories for each occupancy and construction type, with sprinkler increases [unverified — confirm independently]. A floor plate that works in area may still fail on height. Run both before you fall in love with a scheme.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is using remembered or online table values instead of the adopted edition's. The control is a code consultant's written analysis with the actual table values, the frontage measurements from the survey and the formula as adopted. Professional sign-off required: a registered architect or licensed code consultant.

The beginner's mistake

Counting any open ground as frontage. Qualifying open space must meet the code's definitions for width and access, and a neighbour's parking lot you do not control may not qualify or may be built on later.

Callback

In Week 17, Sage taught reverse engineering a deal from public information: start from the price and work back to the implied rent and return. The same habit works on the code: start from the floor plate the deal needs and work back to what the code would demand.

Recap

Start from the target floor plate, find the shortfall against the tabular area, solve for the frontage factor, convert to feet of open perimeter, and price every route to close any remaining gap. Then check height. Use only the adopted edition's values.

Next: Ivo in The Room: the pre-application meeting where you ask the building official how they will classify a hypothetical short-stay building.
checklist: Write the target floor plate area and its dimensions first.
Get the adopted edition's tabular areas from the code consultant, not from memory.
Calculate the shortfall between target and tabular area.
Solve for the frontage increase factor and convert it to feet of qualifying perimeter.
Check which open spaces truly qualify and will stay open.
Price every route to close the gap: frontage, fire wall, higher type, smaller plate.
Check height in feet and stories as well as area.
Get sign-off from a registered architect or code consultant.
head: Field checklist
speak: I reverse engineer the floor plate. Start with the area the deal needs, say 30,000 square feet on a 700-foot perimeter. Get the adopted code's tabular area for the occupancy and type; in my invented example the sprinklered value is 24,000. The shortfall is 6,000, which must come from the frontage increase. Divide by the nonsprinklered value of 12,000 and I need a factor of 0.5, which with 30-foot open spaces means 75 percent of the perimeter, 525 feet, must face qualifying open space. If the site gives only 350 feet, I get 27,000 and I am 3,000 short. Then I price every route: an open yard, a fire wall, a higher construction type or a smaller plate. On my numbers the fire wall wins. Then I check height. Every real value comes from the adopted edition, confirmed by a code consultant.
terms: Tabular allowable area — the area per story the code's table permits for an occupancy and construction type, before increases.
Frontage increase — an increase in allowable area granted where enough of the perimeter faces qualifying open space.
Open frontage — the part of a building's perimeter facing a street or open space that meets the code's width and access requirements.

hostile.q: Your floor plate only works if the neighbour's lot counts as open frontage. What happens when they build on it?
hostile.a: It does not count in our analysis. We only use frontage on public streets and open space we control, and with that frontage our plate is 3,000 square feet short. We close the gap with a rated fire wall, which is in the estimate. If the neighbour builds tomorrow, our allowable area does not change.

title: The Pre-Application Meeting with the Building Official
summary: A pre-application meeting is where you ask the building official how they will read your code basis before you spend money on full drawings. Learn what to bring, the questions to ask, the lines never to say, and how to record what was said. This scene uses a hypothetical short-stay building.
body:
The cheapest code question is the one you ask the building official before the drawings are done. A well-run pre-application meeting turns the official's reading of your occupancy, construction type and separations from a surprise at plan review into a known input to design.

Recall

Q. In the reverse-engineered floor plate, what do you calculate first?

A. The shortfall between the target floor area and the tabular allowable area, which the frontage increase or another route must close.

Q. What is an alternative method, in code terms?

A. A design not specifically prescribed by the code that the official may approve on demonstrated equivalence, usually supported by an engineer's analysis.

Q. What is the owner's role at a design stage gate?

A. To review cost, scope and risk and decide whether the design proceeds, is revised or stops.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, plan review comments arrive months into design, when changes are expensive. Many building departments offer an earlier conversation. It is the best value meeting in the whole code process, and owners who attend it themselves learn more in an hour than in a stack of consultant memos.

The scene

This is a hypothetical building, not your project: a mid-rise with ground-floor retail and serviced residential units above, some to be let for short stays. Present: the building official, a plans examiner, the fire marshal's representative, your architect, your code consultant and you. Your code consultant has sent a two-page code basis a week before: proposed occupancies, construction type, allowable and actual area and height, sprinkler standard, separations, and three questions.

The question behind the question

The official is asking, silently: is this owner straight with me, and will I be cleaning up a misclassification after occupancy? Your real question is: how will this department read the line between transient and non-transient use for our model? Everything you say should serve both.

The lines to say

"Thank you for the time. We would like your reading on three points so we design to it rather than argue about it later."

"Our business model is this: a mix of monthly leases and stays of less than a week, managed from a front desk. Given that, we have classified the residential floors as transient. Does the department agree?"

"If the share of short stays changes in operation, at what point would the department consider it a change of occupancy?"

"We propose separating the retail from the residential with rated assemblies. Is there anything in your local amendments we should know about?"

"May we send you a short note of what we understood today, for you to correct if we have it wrong?"

Say that out loud now.

Here is how we intend to operate. How will you classify it?

The lines never to say

Never say "Other cities let us do this." It tells the official you are shopping for a lenient reading. Never say "It is basically apartments" when your pro forma says otherwise, because Rule 100 exists for exactly this. Never ask for a commitment the official cannot give: pre-application advice is usually informal and not binding, and pressing for a promise damages the relationship. And never let your consultant argue an interpretation in the room; take it away and respond in writing.

When to stay silent

After you describe the business model and ask how it will be classified, stop. Let the official think aloud. The reasoning you hear, which provisions they look at, what worries them, is more valuable than the conclusion, because it tells you what the plans examiner will check.

Two worked exchanges

Worked example 1. The official says the residential floors will be reviewed as transient, and adds that the department expects the transient accessibility provisions to apply. You reply: "Understood. We will design to that." Your architect confirms afterwards that the number of accessible units rises; on a hypothetical 120-unit building, adding six more accessible units with larger bathrooms might cost about 15,000 dollars each, 90,000 dollars, which is far cheaper now than after drawings are complete.

Worked example 2. The plans examiner questions whether the retail separation is needed at all, suggesting nonseparated treatment. Your code consultant starts to argue. You step in: "That is helpful. We will look at both approaches and send you a comparison." Back at the office, the comparison shows nonseparated treatment would impose stricter requirements across the residential floors. You keep the separation and explain why in writing.

Holding your state

You may hear an answer that costs money. Write it down, thank them, and do not negotiate in the room. A calm owner who says "we will design to your reading" earns goodwill that matters at plan review, inspections and the certificate of occupancy.

Working with advisers

This month's thread: the code consultant is the adviser whose value is easiest to underrate. You pay for an hour that prevents months, and you rarely see the problem that did not happen. Hire one at concept stage for anything beyond a simple building, give them the real business model rather than the one that sounds best, and ask them to tell you what the official is likely to worry about.

Then judge them by a simple test after each meeting: did their written basis predict what the official said? An adviser whose predictions keep matching the official's reading is worth keeping. One who keeps being surprised is costing you more than their fee.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is presenting a business model to the official that differs from the one you will operate. The control is a pre-application package that states the real operating model, followed by a written note of the meeting. Professional sign-off required: the registered architect and code consultant who prepared the basis.

The beginner's mistake

Sending only the consultant. The official reads the owner, and the owner learns what the drawings will need.

Callback

In Week 6, Kema taught "I will confirm by Friday" and the acknowledge, bridge, answer method for hostile questions. A pre-application meeting rewards both: acknowledge the official's concern, take the argument away, and confirm in writing by the date you promised.

Recap

Send the code basis ahead, state the real business model, ask how it will be classified, listen to the reasoning, never argue in the room, and confirm in writing.

Next: Kema on Quiz and Recap: six questions on the code basis, Cole's Auditor's Chair and a boardroom drill.
checklist: Send a two-page code basis and your questions a week before the meeting.
Attend yourself, with the architect and code consultant.
Describe the real operating model, including length of stay.
Ask how the department will classify it and when a change would trigger a new permit.
Ask about local amendments that affect your basis.
Do not argue interpretations in the room; respond in writing.
Send a written note of what you understood for the official to correct.
head: Field checklist
speak: The pre-application meeting is the cheapest code advice I will ever get. A week before, my code consultant sends a two-page code basis: occupancies, construction type, allowable and actual height and area, sprinklers, separations and three questions. In the room I state the real operating model, including how long guests stay, and I ask how the department will classify it and at what point a change in operation would become a change of occupancy. Then I stay silent and listen to the reasoning, because it tells me what plan review will check. I never say other cities allow it, I never call short stays apartments, and I never press for a binding promise. If an answer costs money, I say we will design to it. Afterwards I send a written note of what we understood for the official to correct.
terms: Pre-application meeting — an early, usually informal meeting with the building department to discuss a project before formal submission.
Plans examiner — the building department reviewer who checks permit drawings against the adopted code.
Code analysis — the written statement of a building's occupancy, construction type, height and area, separations and fire protection under the adopted code.

hostile.q: The building official's reading in the meeting raised your accessible unit count. Why did you not fight it?
hostile.a: Because the reading was reasonable for a transient building and it came at concept stage, when six more accessible units cost about 90,000 dollars to design in. Fighting it would have risked the relationship we need at plan review, inspections and occupancy, and if we lost later the cost would have been several times higher. We designed to it and confirmed it in writing.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 100 Review: The Code Basis on One Page
summary: Six questions test the week: the four code-basis answers, transient occupancy, construction types, the adopted edition, alternatives and reverse engineering a floor plate. Cole takes the Auditor's Chair to read a hypothetical code analysis sheet as a hostile auditor would. A two-minute boardroom drill closes the week.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: four code answers, occupancy, construction type, height and area, and mixed use, decided honestly from the real business model, written on one page under the adopted edition, and changed only by the owner.

Recall

Q. What is a frontage increase?

A. An increase in allowable area granted where enough of the building's perimeter faces qualifying open space.

Q. What should you never say in a pre-application meeting?

A. That other cities allow it, that short stays are basically apartments, or anything that presses the official for a binding promise.

Q. What is a probate, in concept?

A. The court process that confirms a will and the executor's authority to deal with a deceased person's assets. Its rules vary by jurisdiction; verify against the primary source.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the code basis is short to write and expensive to get wrong. Answer each question aloud before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. Name the four code-basis answers in order.

Answer: Occupancy, construction type, allowable height and area, and the treatment of mixed uses.

Question 2. What usually separates group R-1 from group R-2?

Answer: Whether occupants are transient, typically decided by length of stay; hotels are R-1, apartments and condominiums R-2. Confirm the definition in the adopted code.

Question 3. Why do many mid-rise buildings combine a concrete podium with wood framing above?

Answer: To use the cheaper construction type wherever the code allows it, while the noncombustible podium carries parking and retail and is treated separately from the floors above.

Question 4. Which code edition governs a project?

Answer: The adopted edition with local amendments in force when a complete permit application is filed, subject to local transition rules.

Question 5. How should you price an alternative method?

Answer: As an option that may be refused, with a fallback design already drawn and priced.

Question 6. What is Rule 100?

Answer: Classify the building on how it will actually be used, rented and sold, and treat any change of use as a code, zoning, loan and insurance event before it becomes a marketing decision.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Ivo set out the four code-basis answers. Ford took a composite case of apartments that became a hotel and gave Rule 100. Priya priced construction type, area limits and separations in cost, revenue and equity. REGA traced adoption, editions, the official's authority, alternatives, appeals and the existing building code. Ivo reverse engineered a floor plate from the area the code allows. Ivo ran the pre-application meeting.

Cole's Auditor's Chair

Week 100 is a fourth week, so the Red Pen becomes Cole's Auditor's Chair: read this hypothetical code analysis sheet, taken from a drawing cover, as a hostile auditor would. Find the defects before reading on.

Code analysis. Code: International Building Code, latest edition. Occupancy: R-2 residential (operator to offer nightly and weekly stays). Ground floor: restaurant, nonseparated. Construction type: V-A throughout. Allowable area per story: 30,000 square feet including frontage on all four sides. Actual area per story: 30,000 square feet. Sprinklers: yes. Height: within limits. Alternative methods: none required. Prepared by: design team.

The defects. First, "latest edition" is not a code basis; the governing document is the adopted edition with local amendments, and it must be named. Second, the occupancy says R-2 while the note promises nightly stays, which is the Rule 100 contradiction on the cover sheet itself. Third, the restaurant is nonseparated, so its requirements would apply throughout, yet the sheet shows no sign that anyone checked what that means for the residential floors. Fourth, frontage on all four sides is claimed with no widths and no evidence that each side qualifies or will stay open. Fifth, actual area equals allowable area exactly, which leaves no margin and invites the question of whether the number was reverse fitted. Sixth, "sprinklers: yes" names no standard; the sprinkler standard chosen changes what the building may do. Seventh, "height: within limits" gives no numbers for feet or stories. Eighth, "prepared by design team" names no licensed person; an auditor asks who signs and takes responsibility.

Then the auditor asks for evidence. The ordinance adopting the code. The operator's business plan with lengths of stay. The separation comparison for the restaurant. The survey showing frontage widths. The table values used and their source. The sprinkler standard and its design basis. The height calculation. The name and licence of the code consultant or architect who prepared it. A code sheet that cannot produce its evidence in an hour is a sheet the plans examiner will take apart.

The boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes to an investor who asks, "Why did the code change our building?" Then compare.

Model answer: "The code sorts every building by four answers. What it is used for: because we are letting units for short stays, it is a transient occupancy, which adds accessible units and alarm features. What it is built of: a concrete podium with wood framing above, so each part uses the cheapest type the code allows. How tall and big it may be: the wood floors hit an area cap, so we added a rated fire wall, which was cheaper than any other route and recovered the lost revenue. And how the uses fit together: the restaurant is separated so its rules do not spread upstairs. We met the building official early, designed to their reading and confirmed it in writing. Nothing in the plan depends on an approval we do not have."

Score yourself. Did you open with the bottom line? Did you name all four answers? Did you give one number? Did you finish inside two minutes? If not, record it again tomorrow.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is a code basis that describes a different building from the one you will operate. The control is the one-page basis stating the operating model, signed by a registered architect or code consultant, and confirmed with the official.

The beginner's mistake

Treating the cover sheet as a formality. It is the first page the plans examiner and every later buyer's consultant will read.

Callback

In Week 83, Cole taught audit and critique: reading your own team's work as an outsider would. The Auditor's Chair is that discipline applied to one sheet of paper, and it is the cheapest review you will ever run.

Recap

Occupancy, construction type, height and area, mixed use; adopted edition, alternatives with fallbacks, reverse-engineered floor plates and an honest pre-application meeting. Rule 100 ties the code to the real business model.

Next: Cyrus on First Principles: egress and accessibility, travel distance, exits and accessible routes and units.
checklist: Name the four code-basis answers in order.
What usually separates group R-1 from group R-2?
Why do many mid-rise buildings combine a concrete podium with wood framing above?
Which code edition governs a project?
How should you price an alternative method?
What is Rule 100?
head: The six questions
speak: This week was the code basis on one page. Four answers in order: occupancy, construction type, height and area, and mixed use. Occupancy follows the real business model, so short stays usually make a building transient, group R-1, rather than apartments, group R-2. Construction type sets cost and limits, which is why many buildings put wood over a concrete podium. Area caps are revenue caps, and I price every route around them, a fire wall, more frontage, a higher type or a smaller plate. The adopted edition with local amendments governs, fixed by when a complete application is filed, and the official may approve alternatives on demonstrated equivalence, so every alternative carries a fallback. I meet the official early, state the real operating model and confirm in writing. Rule 100: classify on actual use, and treat any change of use as a code, zoning, loan and insurance event.
terms: Code of record — the adopted code edition and amendments that govern a particular project.
Cover sheet — the first drawing in a set, usually carrying the project data and the code analysis.
Sprinkler standard — the referenced standard, such as NFPA 13 or one of its residential variants, that sets how a sprinkler system is designed.

hostile.q: Your code sheet says latest edition, R-2 and nightly stays. Which of those is true?
hostile.a: None of them is acceptable as written, and I am replacing the sheet. The code basis will name the adopted edition and amendments in force at our application date. The occupancy will match the operating model in the business plan, and if we offer nightly stays, that is transient and the design follows. Every number will have its source, and the sheet will be signed by the licensed code consultant.
